JSON: Name: ai_inclusive_women_tourism Title: A randomized controlled mixed-methods evaluation of a responsible gender-aware AI toolkit to increase inclusivity and business performance of women entrepreneurs in tourism Short Hypothesis: Deployment of a responsible, gender-aware AI toolkit (including bias mitigation, transparency features, and human-in-the-loop controls) causes a statistically significant increase in business performance and perceived inclusivity among women-led tourism microenterprises compared with both (a) no-AI and (b) non-gender-aware AI baselines over a six-month intervention period. Related Work: Prior work divides into three streams: (1) AI as an enabler of SME and tourism business performance via automation, personalized customer interaction, and data-driven decision support; (2) studies of ethical/responsible AI highlighting transparency, privacy, bias mitigation, and human-centric design principles; and (3) qualitative research on barriers to women’s entrepreneurship in tourism (capital, networks, work-life balance). Limitations across these streams include: empirical work focuses on efficiency and customer-facing gains rather than inclusivity outcomes; responsible AI research is largely normative or conceptual with limited field-level causal evaluation; and literature on women in tourism is predominantly qualitative and lacks experimental tests of technology interventions. No existing approach jointly evaluates a gender-aware responsible-AI intervention, measures causal effects on both objective business KPIs and subjective inclusivity outcomes, or performs component-level (ablation) analysis of ethical features in real-world tourism microenterprise settings. Abstract: Problem: Evidence is lacking on whether and how AI can be deployed responsibly to reduce barriers and increase inclusivity for women entrepreneurs in tourism. Approach: We propose a randomized controlled mixed-methods field experiment deploying a packaged responsible, gender-aware AI toolkit for women-led tourism microenterprises. The toolkit integrates algorithmic bias mitigation, actionable transparency (explainable outputs and provenance logs), human-in-the-loop decision controls, and tailored automation for time-consuming operational tasks. Main contribution: The study provides the first causal evaluation of a responsible AI intervention designed explicitly for women entrepreneurs in tourism, quantifying effects on objective business performance, time-use, perceived inclusivity, and algorithmic fairness, and decomposing which ethical components drive outcomes via ablation arms. Expected outcome: Results will determine whether responsible AI increases measurable business outcomes and perceived inclusivity relative to non-AI and standard-AI baselines, and will identify which responsible-AI components are necessary for inclusive impact. Experiments: Population and sampling: 180 women-led tourism microenterprises (sole proprietors or firms with <=10 employees) recruited across three countries representing diverse regulatory and infrastructure contexts; stratified randomization by country and firm size. Arms (random assignment, n=60 per arm): (A) Control: no new AI tools (business-as-usual); (B) Standard-AI: deployment of generic AI toolset (automated chatbots, generic recommender, automated social-media content generation) without gender-aware or transparency modules; (C) Responsible-Gender-AI: same functional tools instrumented with (i) bias-mitigation pipelines (training-data balancing and counterfactual augmentation), (ii) transparency UI exposing provenance, confidence and simple local explanations, and (iii) human-in-the-loop override and audit logs. Ablation sub-arms within (C): remove transparency (C1, n=15), remove bias-mitigation (C2, n=15), remove human-in-the-loop (C3, n=15) to enable component analysis. Data collection: baseline 3 months pre-intervention and 6 months intervention period; datasets include firm-level CRM and booking logs, web/app analytics (impressions, clicks, conversion), time-use diaries (weekly), customer demographics/impressions, system logs (recommendation outputs, provenance), and repeated surveys (perceived inclusivity, trust, workload, Likert scales). Baselines for comparison: Control and Standard-AI arms. Evaluation metrics: primary objective metrics: percentage change in monthly revenue, bookings per month, conversion rate, and mean weekly hours spent on operational tasks; primary subjective metrics: composite Perceived Inclusivity Score and Trust Score (validated Likert scales); algorithmic metrics: disparate impact ratio and exposure parity for women-led offers across customer segments, calibration error, and explanation fidelity. Statistical analysis: intent-to-treat and per-protocol analyses; difference-in-differences for pre/post comparisons; mixed-effects linear models with random intercepts for firms and fixed effects for country; hypothesis tests (ANOVA and pairwise t-tests with Holm correction). Ablation analysis: compare C vs C1/C2/C3 to estimate marginal contribution of transparency, bias-mitigation, and human-in-loop using interaction terms. Qualitative evaluation: semi-structured interviews with purposive subsample (n=30, 10 per arm) and thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Power: target 80% power to detect a standardized effect size d=0.5 on primary revenue metric at alpha=0.05 given n=60 per arm. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: model degradation on domain-specific data, poor recommendation quality, and system outages affecting user adoption. Data biases: training data may encode contextual gendered patterns leading to residual bias despite mitigation; customer demographic sparsity can limit fairness metric reliability. Measurement bias: self-reported perceived inclusivity and time-use diaries are subject to social desirability and recall error. Sample and generalization limits: sample restricted to women-led microenterprises in three countries may not generalize to larger firms, other sectors, or regions with different digital infrastructures. Confounding and externalities: concurrent marketing campaigns or macro shocks (health, political, economic) can confound measured business outcomes. Scalability and compute: real-time personalization and provenance logging increase compute and storage requirements; small firms may lack connectivity to support advanced models. Ethical and regulatory constraints: cross-border data sharing and privacy regulations may restrict dataset completeness and intervention features. Evaluation limitations: six-month intervention may be insufficient to observe long-run structural changes in inclusivity or investor access.
